name: Glassway

detectability.signature: Stratified gravitational gradient; laminar tidal layers; visible as parallel bands of distorted starlight resembling glass panes

proximity: Gravitational instruments detect sharply defined tidal layers—gravity varies in parallel planes
Visible distortion of starfield into horizontal bands, like looking through stacked glass sheets
Mild structural creaking as the ship's hull responds to differential gravity across its height
contact: Ship experiences layered tidal stress—different decks pulled in different directions
Navigation requires precise alignment with tidal planes to minimize cross-layer stress
Objects placed between layers stretch or compress visibly
prolonged_exposure: Cumulative structural fatigue from sustained differential tidal forces
Crew on different decks age at measurably different rates due to gravitational time dilation between layers
Hull material develops micro-fractures along tidal plane boundaries

phenomena: Light bending in parallel stratified layers
Tidal forces causing structural stress along defined planes
Time dilation effects between adjacent tidal layers
Gravitational lensing producing banded distortion of background stars
hazards: Structural collapse from tidal forces if ship crosses layers at wrong angle
Hull breach from sustained cross-layer stress
Differential aging of crew members on different decks during transit
opportunities: Shortcut through normal space—transit along tidal planes is frictionless and fast
Unique research opportunity for studying gravitational stratification
Strategic chokepoint—ships must enter aligned, making approach predictable and defensible
known_incidents: Merchant Captain Aerin Voss discovered in 2581 that ships aligned precisely with the tidal planes could transit the Glassway at speeds exceeding normal drive capacity, as the laminar gravity field acts as a frictionless accelerator; her route shaved three days off the Pale Reaches trade corridor.

A warship squadron attempted to transit the Glassway in battle formation in 2617; three ships entered misaligned with the tidal planes and suffered catastrophic hull failures within seconds as differential gravity tore them apart along deck lines.
description: Glassway is a corridor of stratified gravity 0.3 AU across, where space has been sliced into parallel layers of differing gravitational intensity. Visually, the effect is hauntingly beautiful: starlight passing through the field bends in discrete bands, producing an image like a view through stacked panes of antique glass—each layer slightly offset, slightly distorted, the composite image recognizable but subtly wrong. The layers are precisely defined, with sharp transitions between gravitational intensities that create tidal forces along boundaries as crisp as knife edges.

Transit through the Glassway is a matter of alignment. A ship oriented parallel to the tidal planes—hull flat along the layers—experiences minimal stress, riding the laminar field like a leaf on a river. The gravity gradient actually accelerates vessels along the corridor, making the Glassway one of the fastest natural transit routes in the sector. A ship that enters misaligned, however, places different parts of its hull in different gravitational layers. The tidal stress across a boundary can exceed the tensile strength of military-grade alloys. The warship losses of 2617 demonstrated the consequences with brutal clarity: three vessels sheared apart along their deck lines in seconds.

The Glassway's laminar structure is unique among known gravitational anomalies. Most tidal zones feature smooth gradients; the Glassway's layers are sharp-edged and precisely spaced, as regular as crystalline lattice planes. This regularity has led some theorists to propose that the field is not natural but residual—the gravitational echo of a structure that once existed here, its physical form long gone but its gravitational imprint preserved in spacetime like a fossil in stone. At 2.8 billion years old, whatever created the imprint is beyond recovery, but the pattern it left behind remains perfectly preserved.

Captain Voss's discovery transformed the Glassway from a navigational hazard into a trade artery. Ships aligned with the tidal planes can cross the 0.3 AU corridor in a fraction of the normal transit time, making the Glassway a critical shortcut on the Pale Reaches trade corridor. A small industry of Glassway pilots has emerged—specialists who guide vessels into precise alignment before entry, earning substantial fees for what amounts to a few hours of work with zero margin for error. The Glassway is forgiving of perfection and merciless to anything less. Every pilot knows the three shattered warship hulls still visible in the field, frozen mid-destruction in the tidal layers, a permanent reminder of what happens when alignment is off by even a fraction of a degree.
